what_this_is: Every belief this project held and then measured and lost. Generated from the evidence files each entry cites, so a correction cannot claim a number no report contains. Five of the eight are fixed; three are open and say why.

how_found_legend.benchmark: Benchmarked the obvious answer before building on it
how_found_legend.ablation: Ablated the fusion layer one detector at a time
how_found_legend.third_party: Scored the detector on data this project did not generate
how_found_legend.ran_the_product: Submitted a genuine packet to the running API and read the verdict
how_found_legend.self_attack: Built the attack against our own detector
how_found_legend.reproduced: Regenerated a result and asked why a number had moved

corrections.title: The popular pretrained deepfake checkpoint is at chance on our data
corrections.believed: An off-the-shelf deepfake checkpoint with thousands of downloads is a reasonable baseline to build on.
corrections.measured: Both candidates scored at or below chance on our own images. Their label mappings were verified first, so this is not an inverted-sign bug — it is what happens when a model trained on StyleGAN and face-swap video frames meets diffusion output.
corrections.outcome: The CNN became one vote in an ensemble rather than the system. A project that had shipped the popular checkpoint on reputation would have reported a confident number for a model that was guessing.

corrections.title: Half the headline AUC was a label we wrote into our own files
corrections.believed: The system scores 0.913 held out, and five detectors earned it.
corrections.measured: Ablating one detector at a time showed metadata/EXIF carrying 49.5% of the above-chance AUC — because the corpus generator had conditioned EXIF mode on the label, leaving three modes that appeared on fraudulent packets and never on genuine ones. 17.3% of the corpus carried a fraud label in disguise. Two of the five detectors were making the model actively worse.
corrections.outcome: Corpus regenerated with EXIF mixed across classes. Two independent guards now refuse to build or to ship a corpus in which any EXIF mode lands on one class only, with a single documented exemption for a mode no camera can physically produce. The headline fell 0.16 and is now worth its number.

corrections.title: The calibrator was quietly costing 0.02 AUC
corrections.believed: Calibrating the fused score is free — it changes the scale, not the ranking.
corrections.measured: Isotonic regression on 195 rows fitted a step function with so few levels that held-out scores collapsed to 14 distinct values. AUC measures ranking, and mass ties destroy ranking. It also made the score useless as a dial: a packet a hair above a step boundary jumped from 0.44 to 0.92, while policy.yaml cuts that score at fixed thresholds.
corrections.outcome: Replaced with Platt scaling — two parameters, strictly monotonic, so it preserves ranking exactly and returns a smooth score. Nothing was broken and no test failed; the number was simply lower than the model had earned.

evidence.note: The before-figure was never written to a report; it is recorded in this class's docstring, and this entry says so rather than implying a file.

corrections.title: The identity threshold would have rejected two thirds of honest applicants
corrections.believed: The face-match lower bound was calibrated — it was fitted, on our own pairs.
corrections.measured: Graded against LFW's 6,000 real pairs, the corpus-fitted bound accepts 32.23% of genuine pairs. The corpus could not have revealed this: its 'two photographs of one person' are one photograph re-captured twice, scoring 0.943, where two genuinely different photographs of the same person score 0.758.
corrections.metric: True-accept rate on real LFW pairs
corrections.outcome: The bound is fitted on LFW's official 10-fold protocol and calibrate.py no longer overwrites it with the corpus value. Fitting this bound on this corpus produces a wrong answer every time, and a worse one the better the corpus gets at making one person's two images look alike.

corrections.title: Every genuine applicant false-linked to a stranger
corrections.believed: Linkage catches onboarding rings, and its threshold was fitted on LFW at a strict false-accept budget.
corrections.measured: The threshold was fitted for a *pair* and deployed as a *search*. Against the shipped 5,000-record scan limit, 99.99% of genuine applicants pick up a false link. A pairwise false-accept rate applied N times compounds; the pair fit stays where it was put. LFW's official protocol cannot resolve this — 3,000 impostor pairs bottom out at 3.3e-4, and the shipped rate was two pairs.
corrections.metric: Genuine applicants false-linking over a 5,000-record scan
corrections.outcome: Refitted over all 16,522,626 impostor pairs among LFW's distinct identities, from a stated 1% budget. A face link can also no longer reject anyone by itself — it is capped one abstention band below the reject threshold, and only a byte-identical file is exempt. The cost is stated: true-accept falls from 95.13% to 38.53%.

corrections.title: The frequency head separates real Indian faces from real FFHQ faces
corrections.believed: The spectral head is this project's best detector — 0.969 train AUC on detecting synthesis.
corrections.measured: Scored on two groups that are *both genuine* — real photographs of Indian people against real FFHQ photographs, geometry-controlled — it separates them at 0.9155. It learned the prompt list: every synthetic face in our corpus was generated from a prompt naming the demographic, and FFHQ is predominantly not South Asian. The pretrained CNN scores 0.5007 on the same comparison — exactly chance, and the only component here with no demographic signal at all.
corrections.metric: Shortcut AUC, real vs real (0.5 is the only defensible value)
corrections.outcome: Nothing has been tuned in response, deliberately. The corpus needs rebuilding with demography decoupled from the label and the head refitting on it. Adjusting a threshold until the table looks better would move the disparity somewhere a metric cannot see, which is the failure this measurement exists to report.

corrections.title: The selfie detector does not work on fakes we did not generate
corrections.believed: The selfie detector catches diffusion output at 0.997 — the one attack class this project had solved.
corrections.measured: Scored on four generator families from two third-party datasets, geometry-controlled and reported per family rather than pooled, it is at or below chance on every one of them. The worst, stylegan, is at 0.1234 — below 0.5 means inverted: it scores those fakes as more genuine than real faces. The 0.997 was the detector reading its own generator's settings.
corrections.metric: ROC-AUC per generator family, controlled face protocol
corrections.outcome: This is the most consequential finding in the project and it is unresolved. It does not sink the system — the fused verdict rests on provenance, structural document checks and behaviour, not on this detector, and the ablation already showed it carrying 10.6% of above-chance AUC rather than the headline. But a detector marketed on deepfake detection that is at chance on somebody else's deepfakes has to say so in its own README.

corrections.title: We built the attack that defeats our own behavioral detector
corrections.believed: Keystroke rhythm is the one signal a fraud kit cannot buy — 1.000 held-out AUC against every automation strategy we had.
corrections.measured: A replay attacker that dispatches a *real* person's recorded dwell and flight timings through the devtools protocol — rollover included, by laying presses and releases on a timeline rather than emitting them key by key — scores 0.4996. Chance. Nothing about its rhythm is synthetic.
corrections.outcome: Not fixable by a better rhythm model: the rhythm genuinely is human. What Detector 6 buys is raising the cost of automating a KYC form from free to 'you must first record a real human filling one'. The roadmap item is that a replayed recording is a *reused* one, which is the linkage problem this repo already solves for faces and files — not a timing problem.

corrections.title: The stale thresholds could not be fixed by fitting them properly
corrections.believed: The shipped 0.40 and 0.75 are stale because nobody re-fitted them. Refit them on the training split with cross-validation — never touching held-out — and the problem goes away.
corrections.measured: The procedure works and the corpus cannot support it. The chosen reject point (0.66) holds a 2.02% false-positive rate out-of-fold and produces 17.65% on a split it was not chosen on — 8.7x optimistic. Every training identity is distinct, so this is not fold leakage; 195 genuine faces simply cannot resolve an operating point that survives new faces.
corrections.metric: False-positive rate at the chosen reject threshold
corrections.outcome: So the defaults do not come from cross-validation. They come from the system's own cost curve, which priced the shipped 0.75 reject line at negative expected net benefit and put its argmax at 0.80 — moving there took the false-reject rate from 9.8% to 2.0% and precision from 0.815 to 0.952. The review line, which the cost model does not cover, moved from 0.40 to 0.45 because 0.40 sat barely above the genuine median and sent 39% of honest merchants to a human. Both are read off held-out, so they report themselves: an operating point, not a generalisation claim. The mechanism that matters is still per-merchant policy plus the cost curve, and the defaults are only a sane place to start.
